children: India's Enforcement Directorate told Ebix not to create any lien on its assets. Ebix’s Australian arm has now borrowed A$41 million against them, a BW investigation shows. It is the second Ebix asset known to be pledged since the freeze.
Imagine a court freezes your house.

You cannot sell it, gift it or mortgage it until your case is decided. Now imagine you walk into a lender’s office anyway, pledge the house, and leave with the cash. If you lose the case, the state takes the house. But the lender gets paid first. The state gets whatever is left.

That is, in plain terms, what has now happened twice with assets the ED froze in the Mahadev betting-app money-laundering case. ED has claimed that the Nasdaq listed company Ebix was purchased with laundered or Hawala money from the Mahadev Betting Scandal.
The New Loan
Ebix Australia Pty Ltd, a subsidiary of US-based Ebix Inc, has taken a A$41 million (about Rs 271 crore) senior secured loan from Sydney private-credit firm iPartners.
This has not been reported before.
iPartners lists the deal on its investor portal as the “EBIX Australia Secured Corporate Loan (EBIX02)”. According to the listing:
the loan runs three years, with 34 months remaining, which places its start around August 2026;
the security is “first ranking”;
the loan-to-value ratio is below 30%;
it pays one-month BBSW plus 5.50% a year, which iPartners puts at an effective 9.82%;
the investor offering is closed.
What does this mean in plain English?
“First ranking” means the lender stands at the front of the queue for Ebix Australia’s assets.

A loan-to-value ratio below 30% means those assets are worth more than three times the loan, so the lender is very well protected. Anyone else with a claim, including the Indian government, stands behind it.
iPartners pitched the borrower to its investors as “a mature, highly cashflow positive market-dominant InsurTech business.” In other words, one of the best assets the group has left.
What the ED Ordered
On June 5, 2026, the ED’s Raipur zonal office issued Provisional Attachment Order No.

16/2026. It attached Rs 893 crore of the shareholding that Vikas Garg’s listed company, Eraaya Lifespaces (since renamed Ebix Ltd), holds in Ebix Inc. The order covered the shares “including all the assets and investments of the said company.”

A copy went to Ebix Inc’s promoter and managing director “with a direction not to allow any sale/transfer/alienate/modification/creating lien etc. in respect of assets of M/s EBIX Inc and its subsidiaries.”
Ebix Australia is a subsidiary of Ebix Inc. A first-ranking security over its assets is a lien.

The ED saw this coming. Its order warned that the assets “may be sold, transferred or encumbered in order to create third-party interests,” and called the Ebix shareholding “susceptible to swift inter-corporate transfer, pledging or encumbrance.”
The Pattern
Garg was arrested on July 14, 2026.
Three weeks later, on August 4, Ebix Inc pledged its 17-acre headquarters at 1 Ebix Way, Johns Creek, Georgia, to Velocity Commercial Capital for a US$12.6 million loan, as BW reported earlier.
The deed is recorded in Georgia’s land records at Deed Book 70417.
The Australian facility began in the same month.

Here is how the game works. India froze the shares at the top of the group, held by the Indian listed company. But the real assets, the buildings, the software businesses and the cash flows, sit at the bottom, in the US and Australia.
An Indian freeze order does not automatically bind a Georgia land registry or a Sydney lender. To enforce it abroad, India must go through slow treaty channels.
In that gap, the assets underneath can be borrowed against, one by one.

The frozen shares still exist on paper. But each new first-ranking loan means the business those shares represent is worth less to anyone who comes after the lender, including a government trying to confiscate it.

In its supplementary prosecution complaint filed in Raipur in September, the ED told the court that after its attachment order Garg “tried to sell” the Georgia campus through broker Cresa, and called it a knowing attempt to “dissipate the proceeds of crime.” The complaint does not mention either the US mortgage or the Australian loan.
Where the Money Goes
Ebix Australia has long been one of the group’s healthier units.
When Eraaya completed its takeover in 2024, its then managing director, the late Leon d’Apice, said: “The Australian operation remains profitable and strong.” It is now led by Philip Fourie.
The parent is in far worse shape. Eraaya reported a consolidated loss of Rs 326 crore for the quarter ended September 2025, and its consolidated net worth turned negative.
A person with knowledge of the company’s finances told BW the loan was raised to clear dues owed to the Australian Taxation Office under a tax settlement.

That settlement limited how much money Ebix Australia could send to group companies overseas. Once the ATO was paid, the person said, cash from Australia could flow to Ebix’s loss-making units in India and the US.
Short-seller Viceroy Research reported in 2018 that the ATO had been auditing Ebix since at least 2016.
If that account is right, the group’s strongest business has been borrowed against so its cash can move to weaker ones.
Moving money across the group is exactly what the ED’s order was meant to stop.
Silence
BW could not find any public disclosure of the Ebix Australia loan by Ebix Ltd, the listed parent.
The ED froze the shares.
The assets beneath them are being pledged, one country at a time.
Palak Shah

BW Reporters Palak Shah is a seasoned investigative journalist and the fearless author of The Market Mafia: Chronicle of India’s High-Tech Stock Market Scandal & The Cabal That Went Scot-Free, a hard-hitting exposé that unmasked the shadowy underbelly of India’s financial markets.

With nearly two decades of boots-on-the-ground reporting in Mumbai, Palak has carved a reputation as a relentless truth-seeker, diving deep into the nexus of money, power, and regulation. His bylines have graced India’s most prestigious financial dailies, including The Economic Times, Business Standard, The Financial Express, and The Hindu Business Line, where his incisive coverage has shaped narratives and rattled boardrooms.

Drawn to crime reporting at the tender age of 19, Palak quickly realized that Mumbai’s gritty gang wars of the 1980s had given way to a slicker, more insidious form of organized crime—white-collar schemes orchestrated in corporate towers. This epiphany fueled his pivot to financial journalism, where he’s spent years decoding the complex machinations of India’s ‘white money’ economy.

From stock market manipulations to regulatory loopholes, Palak’s work peels back the polished veneer of high finance to reveal the cabals pulling the strings. His passion for uncovering truth, backed by a knack for connecting dots others miss, makes him a formidable voice in Indian journalism, unafraid to challenge the status quo and expose the players who think they’re untouchable.
